newsitem.title: USA: TV industry agrees to new voluntary ratings system.
newsitem.headline: TV industry agrees to new voluntary ratings system.

text.p: Major U.S. television networks and cable broadcasters agreed on Wednesday to modify the current age-based ratings system to better identify programme content, avoiding a threat by Congress to pass a law mandating changes.
The ABC, CBS and Fox networks agreed to the changes, but NBC was still holding out, lawmakers said.
The new system -- to take effect Oct. 1 -- will add content ratings to the existing age-based ratings, including the letter S for sex, L for language, V for violence and D for suggestive dialogue.
Sen. John McCain, an Arizona Republican, announced the agreement in principle, reached on Wednesday by parent groups and negotiators for the television industry.
The agreement expanding the voluntary ratings system initially implemented in January will be signed at a White House ceremony early Thursday, congressional aides said.
President Bill Clinton was out of the country, but Vice President Al Gore played a leading role in keeping the negotiations on track.
"I think this is a great victory for the parents, this is a family victory," McCain said. "This agreement is a done deal, it will be formally signed tomorrow morning, and I am very happy about it."
An aide to McCain said the industry group representing cable television stations would sign the deal, but some specific cable stations had not agreed to the ratings.

The ratings are designed to work in conjunction with the V-chip, a piece of microcircuitry that will be inside of almost every new television set starting next year. Using the V-chip, parents will someday be able to programme their sets to screen out any programme rated beyond a desired level.

Parents' groups and other organisations including the American Medical Association mounted a campaign to revise the ratings system implemented in January, arguing that ratings such as "TV-PG", or parental guidance suggested, did not give enough information about programme content.

Executives from the National Cable Television Association, National Association of Broadcasters and the Motion Picture Association bowed to the pressure and agreed to change the ratings system after an emotional town meeting in Peoria, Illinois, on May 19, where 300 families expressed their concerns about the ratings.

Congressional aides said the advocacy groups and the television executives, who have been negotiating the new ratings system for several weeks, clinched the deal after lawmakers gave the industry written assurances that they would not pursue legislation on programme content for "a substantial period."

"It was a gentleman's agreement. We have given our commitment and our word that we are not going to come back and haunt them every six months," said Ken Johnson, spokesman for Representative Billy Tauzin, the Lousiana Republican who organised the May town meeting.

McCain and other senators, including Republican Leader Trent Lott of Mississippi, said they would recommend that the Federal Communications Commission move expeditiously to approve the revised guidelines.
Tauzin said he hoped NBC would eventually agree to the ratings system, especially once it saw that lawmakers were honouring their moratorium on new legislation.

He said the fact that the ratings system was voluntary was crucial, especially in light of last month's decision by the Supreme Court to overturn a law passed by Congress banning pornography on the Internet. "When you get an agreement, nobody sues," Tauzin said.
He said the revised ratings guidelines would allow viewers to identify offensive or violent programming and turn it off.
"If Americans really want less violence on television, with this agreement, they'll have the tool now to stop it," he said.
